headline: Zei, “tax”, is from Middle Chinese 稅, first cited in Japanese to a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 719.
Kotobazukai is 言葉 (“word”) plus 遣い (“way of using”).
Hanbāgu is shortened from ハンバーグステーキ (hanbāgu sutēki), from English Hamburg steak, first cited to 1941.
Tane is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tanay.
Afurika is ultimately from Latin Āfrica.
Rūru is from English rule.
Arashi has competing theories: 荒ら (ara, “desolate, sparse”) plus 風 (shi, “wind”), or the stem of 荒らす (arasu, “destroy, ruin”).
O, “tail”, was wo in Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE in the senses “tail” and “foot of a mountain”.
Ensō is 演 (“perform,” “put on”) plus 奏 (“play (music)”).
Kūkō is 空 (kū, “air, sky”) plus 港 (kō, “port”).
Konaida contracts このあいだ (kono aida), first cited in 1563.
Komugi is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 麦 (mugi, “dry-cultivated cereal grain”).
Chanto has a hypothetical etymology: possibly a sound shift from 順当 (juntō, “properly, in a smooth way”).
Kaburu is a contraction of 被る (kagafuru), the medial g voicing p to b.
In shitai, 死 is a daiyōji replacing 屍.
Kitaku is 帰 (ki, “return”) plus 宅 (taku, “home”).
Kyōshuku is 恐 (kyō, “awful, fear”) plus 縮 (shuku, “shrink”).
I, “strange”, is from Middle Chinese 異 (MC yiH).
Kin went from kimʉ to kiɴ, from Middle Chinese 金 (kim).
Mochiageru is mochi, the stem of 持つ (motsu, “to hold”), plus 上げる (ageru, “to raise, to lift”).
Zatsuon is 雑 (“miscellaneous”) plus 音 (“sound”).
In kikin, 飢 is a daiyōji replacing 饑.
Shinkansen is 新 (“new”) plus 幹線 (“main line”).
Tsume is from Proto-Japonic *tumay, the standalone form of tsuma.
Dōse is どう (dō, “how”) plus せ, a clipping of せよ (seyo), the imperative of する (suru).
Ogamu is from older 拝む (orogamu), shifting from wogamu.
Hitsujuhin is 必需 (hitsuju, “need, requirement, essentialness”) plus 品 (-hin, “item, good”).
Shaburu is first attested in 1778.
Hikage is 日 (hi, “sun”) plus 陰 (kage, “shade”).
Kangae is the continuative stem of 考える (kangaeru, “to think”).
